glossary.definition: The sub inside the RFC 8693 act claim: which agent is acting. For the Cedar rule the act claim is an OBJECT such as {"sub": "agent-client-example"} (that is what the real run used). If act were emitted as the text "{}" the rule is believed to find no sub and so never to match (UNVERIFIED: simulated here, not measured).

Cedar is the policy language Privilege uses for its AI policies. An AI policy can forbid one tool call. The template "Restrict a tool to tokens carrying a claim" generates a forbid rule with an unless clause on the token's claims; the contains(...) test inside it was read from a real tenant on 2026-11-16. This template's rule is a .contains() test, not a pattern. Whether the real rule is exact, substring or set membership was not measured (UNVERIFIED).

Per the Privilege console documentation (not re-run in this lab, UNVERIFIED) only an Active policy is enforced and a Candidate policy is not, so a refusal you expected will not happen until the policy is Active.

Claims the gateway demands on the presented token, checked at sign-in on the identity or grant. Believed to do the same job as an act.sub policy, earlier (UNVERIFIED: not tested in this lab or on the real tenant run).

This lab's in-process stand-in for the Privilege gateway. It evaluates one rule shape (a tool, the claim path act.sub, a value it compares exactly). It is not a Cedar engine and it decides nothing real.

sources.title: RFC 8693: OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange
sources.use: Defines the act (actor) claim whose sub the policy reads.

sources.title: Cedar policy language
sources.use: The policy language behind the AI policies; the lab uses one rule shape only.

cards.label: Step 1: baseline, no policy
cards.description: The same token calls CountTool and ListIndexTool on a door with no policy. Both are allowed.

cards.label: Step 2: add two Active act.sub policies
cards.description: Shows the Cedar this lab generates for the template, one policy per tool, one naming the token's own agent and one naming a different agent. Only the contains(...) test was read from the real tenant; the lines around it are UNVERIFIED.

cards.label: Step 3: same token, two tools
cards.description: The policy naming this token's agent lets the call through; the policy naming a different agent value refuses the same token, with JSON-RPC -32600 and the policy's reason. Measured with one real agent; a second agent was not tested.

cards.label: Step 4: remove the policies
cards.description: Delete both policies and the same token is allowed on both tools again.

cards.label: Extra scenarios: act as text, no token, Candidate
cards.description: Three simulated cases, none measured: act emitted as the text "{}" is believed never to match, a call with no token is refused at sign-in in this mock, and a Candidate policy is not enforced per the console documentation (not re-run).

cards.label: Measured on a real tenant, 2026-11-16
cards.description: The result of the real run, shown as static evidence apart from the mock runs, with what was not measured.

stories.title: Baseline
stories.say: No policy: the same token gets both tools. That is what every later step is compared with.

stories.title: Two Active policies
stories.say: Same template, same Cedar shape, different tool and different agent. Only Active is enforced.

stories.title: Same token, two tools
stories.say: Where the policy names this agent the call passes; where it names a different agent the call is refused and the reason names the claim.

stories.title: Remove the policies
stories.say: Delete the policies and the same token is allowed on both tools again: the policy was the only change.

stories.title: Edge cases
stories.say: Three edge cases, simulated and not measured: act as text is believed never to match, no token is refused at sign-in in this mock, and per the console documentation a Candidate is not enforced (not re-run).

stories.title: What was measured
stories.say: One real client with one act.sub and two Active policies: the policy naming a different value refused the same token. In one run the first poll, about 7 seconds after creation, already showed the refusal: one observation, not a propagation time. A second real agent was not measured.
